text: On the same straight-line, two other straight-lines  equal, respectively, to  two (given) straight-lines (which meet) cannot be constructed (meeting) at  a different point on the same side (of the straight-line), but having the same ends as the given straight-lines.      For, if possible, let the two straight-lines $AC$, $CB$, equal to two other straight-lines $AD$, $DB$, respectively, have been constructed on the same straight-line $AB$, meeting at different points, $C$ and $D$, on the same side (of $AB$), and having the same ends (on $AB$).
So $CA$ is equal to $DA$, having the same end $A$ as it,

spans.label: glue
spans.text: , having the same end $A$ as it,

text: and $CB$ is equal to $DB$, having the same end $B$ as it.

spans.label: glue
spans.text: , having the same end $B$ as it.

text: Therefore, since $AC$ is equal to $AD$,  the angle $ACD$ is also equal to angle $ADC$ [Prop.~1.5].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: angle $ACD$ is also equal to angle $ADC$

assertion: angle ADC is greater than angle DCB
angle CDB is much greater than angle DCB

text: Again, since  $CB$ is equal to $DB$, the angle $CDB$ is also equal to angle $DCB$ [Prop.~1.5].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: angle $CDB$ is also equal to angle $DCB$

text: But it was shown that the former (angle) is also much greater (than the latter).
assertion: angle CDB was shown to be much greater than angle DCB

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the former (angle) is also much greater (than the latter)

assertion: contradiction: CDB both equal to and much greater than DCB

text: Thus, on the same straight-line, two other straight-lines equal, respectively, to   two (given) straight-lines  (which meet) cannot be constructed (meeting) at a different point on the same side (of the straight-line), but having the same ends as the given straight-lines. (Which is) the very thing it was required to show.
